lessons.title: Density models and probability areas
lessons.summary: Separate a curve height from probability, and use the complete support.
lessons.objective: Validate and normalise piecewise densities and calculate probabilities as areas.
lessons.before: Review definite integration, non-negative functions and interval notation. Some written questions continue into CDFs and quantiles and moments; return to those parts after the relevant lesson.
lessons.ideas:
A height is not a point probability

A density f distributes probability across intervals. For a variable with a density,

\[\mathrm P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.\]

The value f(a) is a height, whereas the probability of the single point X=a is zero. A density may exceed 1; its total area, rather than its maximum height, must be 1. Adding or removing one endpoint from an event does not change its probability.

Two tests are needed

\[f(x)\ge0\quad\text{on the support},\qquad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,dx=1.\]

Normalisation alone does not rule out a negative section. Solve for unknown coefficients, then check the sign on every piece. Values outside the stated support contribute no probability.

Piecewise does not mean continuous

Split an integral at every formula change and at any gap in the support. A continuous random variable need not have a continuous density. Equate adjacent density heights only when the question explicitly imposes that extra condition. A density's value at an isolated endpoint may be reassigned without changing the model.

Read the model before naming a distribution

If an exponential expression is supplied, obtain its probabilities by integration or from the supplied CDF. No memorised mean, median or named-distribution property is required in this chapter.
lessons.method:
1. Write all support intervals and formula changes.
  2. Impose total area 1 and any stated area or matching conditions.
  3. Check each resulting piece is non-negative.
  4. Intersect the requested event with the support and split the integral.
  5. Check the resulting probability lies between 0 and 1.
mistakes: A density height can exceed 1; a probability cannot.
A single point has probability zero, not f at that point.
Do not impose continuity of the density unless it is stated.
Do not integrate one branch across a different branch or a gap.

examples.title: 1 · Normalise before using a height
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=k(2+x)\) for \(0\le x\le1\), and zero otherwise. Find k, f(1), and \(\mathrm P(\frac14\lt X\lt\frac34)\).
examples.solution:
Total area gives \(k[2x+x^2/2]_0^1=5k/2=1\), so \(k=2/5\). The height \(f(1)=6/5\) exceeds 1 and is permitted. The interval probability is

\[\frac25[2x+x^2/2]_{1/4}^{3/4}=\frac12.\]

The probability at the point X=1 itself is zero.

examples.title: 2 · Solve areas without inventing a matching condition
examples.question: A density is \(ax\) on \([0,1)\), b on \([1,3]\), and zero elsewhere. Given \(\mathrm P(X\lt1)=\frac13\), find a and b. Must the two density heights agree at 1?
examples.solution: The first area is a/2=1/3, so a=2/3. Total area gives a/2+2b=1, hence b=1/3. Both branches are non-negative. The left-hand height at 1 is 2/3, while the right-hand height is 1/3. A jump in this density is allowed; no matching condition was given.

examples.title: 3 · Use the correct part of a curved density
examples.question: The density is \(cx(4-x)\) on \([0,4]\), zero otherwise. Find c and \(\mathrm P(X\gt3)\).
examples.solution:
The integral of x(4−x) on [0,4] is 32/3, so c=3/32. The factors x and 4−x are non-negative throughout the support. Thus

\[\mathrm P(X>3)=\frac3{32}[2x^2-x^3/3]_3^4=\frac5{32}.\]

This is an area; substituting x=3 into the density would not give the requested probability.

examples.title: 4 · An event can cross an empty interval
examples.question: A density is 2 on \([0,\frac14]\), \(\frac12\) on \([1,2]\), and zero otherwise. Check it is valid and find \(\mathrm P(\frac15\lt X\lt\frac65)\).
examples.solution:
Both pieces are positive and their areas are 1/2 and 1/2. For the event, only [1/5,1/4] and [1,6/5] contribute:

\[2\left(\frac14-\frac15\right)+\frac12\left(\frac65-1\right)=\frac15.\]

The gap (1/4,1) contributes zero; it is not filled by either formula.

lessons.title: CDFs, quantiles and conditional probabilities
lessons.summary: Accumulate probability across each piece, then choose the correct branch of an inverse problem.
lessons.objective: Build complete CDFs and recover densities, percentiles and conditional probabilities.
lessons.before: Complete density models. Review definite integration, quadratic equations, logarithms and conditional probability.
lessons.ideas:
A complete cumulative description

\[F(x)=\mathrm P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^x f(t)\,dt.\]

For a finite support [a,b], give F=0 below a and F=1 above b, as well as each interior branch. On the second piece, retain all the mass accumulated on earlier pieces. The dummy integration variable t keeps the upper limit x distinct.

A CDF is non-decreasing and lies in [0,1]. For a distribution with a density it is continuous, even where the density jumps. Where differentiable, F′=f. A corner or an arbitrary value of f at one point does not create a point mass.

Probabilities from cumulative values

\[\mathrm P(ab)=1-F(b).\]

For example, with a<b inside the support, the conditional upper-tail probability is \((1-F(b))/(1-F(a))\), provided the denominator is positive. Derive it from the event intersection rather than using an unstated model property.

Select a branch before solving

A p-quantile q satisfies F(q)=p for a strictly increasing continuous CDF; a median has p=1/2. Compare p with the cumulative masses at the breakpoints, solve within the correct branch, and reject roots outside it. For a plateau, use the lower-quantile convention \(q_p=\inf\{x:F(x)\ge p\}\); a flat section may mean the equation has more than one solution.

The interquartile range is \(q_{0.75}-q_{0.25}\). Solve each quartile separately, since they may lie in different pieces. Give exact values unless a rounding instruction is present.
lessons.method:
1. Integrate from the left support boundary.
  2. Carry accumulated mass into every later piece.
  3. Include exterior branches and check continuity, endpoints and monotonicity.
  4. For a percentile, identify its branch using breakpoint probabilities.
  5. For a conditional event, divide the intersection probability by the conditioning probability.
mistakes: The integration constant changes between pieces to preserve accumulated mass.
Differentiate a CDF; integrate a density.
A percentile is an x-value, not a probability.
A quartile root must belong to the branch used to obtain it.

examples.title: 1 · Give the exterior branches as well
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac{2x+1}{6}\) on \([0,2]\), zero elsewhere. Find its CDF and \(\mathrm P(1\lt X\le\frac32)\).
examples.solution:
\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{2}}{6} + \frac{x}{6},&0\le x\lt 2\\1,&x\ge 2.\end{cases}\]

The interior integral is \(\int_0^x(2t+1)/6\,dt\). The requested probability is \(F(3/2)-F(1)=5/8-1/3=7/24\). F(0)=0 and F(2)=1 verify both joins.

examples.title: 2 · Quartiles on different pieces
examples.question: A density is x on \([0,1)\), \(\frac14\) on \([1,3]\), and zero elsewhere. Find the interquartile range.
examples.solution:
\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{2}}{2},&0\le x\lt 1\\\frac{x}{4} + \frac{1}{4},&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

F(1)=1/2. The lower quartile therefore uses x²/2=1/4, giving \(q_{0.25}=\sqrt2/2\). The upper uses (x+1)/4=3/4, giving \(q_{0.75}=2\). Hence the interquartile range is \(2-\sqrt2/2\). Both roots are in their selected branches.

examples.title: 3 · Recover a density from an interior CDF
examples.question: The CDF is 0 below 1, \((x-1)^2/9\) on \([1,4)\), and 1 at and above 4. Find the density and \(\mathrm P(2\lt X\le3)\).
examples.solution:
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{2 x}{9} - \frac{2}{9},&1\le x\le 4\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

Differentiation gives the interior density; it is zero elsewhere. The CDF is continuous at both support endpoints, so no atom is present. The interval probability is \(4/9-1/9=1/3\).

examples.title: 4 · Work directly with a supplied exponential expression
examples.question: A reset-cycle duration T has CDF 0 for t<0 and \(1-e^{-t/4}\) for t≥0. Find its 90th percentile and \(\mathrm P(T\gt8\mid T\gt4)\).
examples.solution:
The percentile equation is \(1-e^{-q/4}=9/10\). Thus \(e^{-q/4}=1/10\), giving \(q=4\ln10\). The conditional event is obtained from the two tails:

\[\frac{\mathrm P(T>8)}{\mathrm P(T>4)}=\frac{e^{-2}}{e^{-1}}=e^{-1}.\]

The denominator is positive. No named-distribution property was assumed.

lessons.title: Expectations of functions and variance
lessons.summary: Integrate the requested function against the original density, checking the whole support.
lessons.objective: Calculate expectations and variances of functions without confusing a function of a mean with a mean of a function.
lessons.before: Review normalised densities, integration of powers, and improper integrals where the support or integrand requires them.
lessons.ideas:
The density still belongs to X

\[\mathrm E(h(X))=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}h(x)f_X(x)\,dx.\]

Use every support piece, replacing X by the integration variable x inside h. This method needs no inverse for h and works even when h is not monotone. The expectation exists as a finite real value when the absolute integral is finite; do not ignore a singularity or an infinite tail.

Variance needs two moments of the same variable

\[\operatorname{Var}(h(X))=\mathrm E(h(X)^2)-\bigl(\mathrm E(h(X))\bigr)^2.\]

For h(X)=√X, the first term is E(X). For h(X)=X², it is E(X⁴), not E(X²). A negative variance signals an error, but a positive result alone is not proof that the calculation is correct.

Only affine functions commute with expectation in general

\[\mathrm E(aX+b)=a\mathrm E(X)+b,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X).\]

In general E(h(X)) does not equal h(E(X)). Likewise Var(√X) is not √Var(X), and E(1/X) is not 1/E(X). When applying a given moment, check whether it is the first or second moment of the variable actually requested.
lessons.method:
1. Name the transformed quantity h(X).
  2. Integrate h(x)f(x) on every original support interval.
  3. For variance, separately integrate h(x)²f(x).
  4. Check convergence and combine the moments exactly.
  5. Round only the final requested quantity.
mistakes: Do not substitute h(x) into the density in place of multiplying by it.
Var(X²) needs the fourth moment of X.
E(√X) is generally not √E(X).
A singular integrand requires a convergence check, even if a single point has probability zero.

examples.title: 1 · Keep the first and second moments separate
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac{3x^2}{8}\) on \([0,2]\), zero elsewhere. Find \(\mathrm E(X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).
examples.solution:
\[\mathrm E(X)=\frac38\int_0^2x^3\,dx=\frac32,\qquad\mathrm E(X^2)=\frac38\int_0^2x^4\,dx=\frac{12}5.\]\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{12}5-\left(\frac32\right)^2=\frac3{20}.\]

The density integrates to 1. Both moments are finite on its bounded support.

examples.title: 2 · Variance after a square root
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac{2(x+1)}{15}\) on \([0,3]\), zero elsewhere. Find \(\mathrm E(\sqrt X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)\).
examples.solution:
\[\mathrm E(\sqrt X)=\frac2{15}\int_0^3(x^{3/2}+x^{1/2})\,dx=\frac{56\sqrt3}{75}.\]

Since (√X)²=X, the other moment is E(X)=9/5. Hence

\[\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)=\frac95-\left(\frac{56\sqrt3}{75}\right)^2=\frac{239}{1875}.\]

Integrating the fractional power is valid at 0: its absolute integral is finite.

examples.title: 3 · A reciprocal with a safe lower endpoint
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=\frac{2x}{3}\) on \([1,2]\), zero elsewhere. Find \(\mathrm E(1/X)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(1/X)\).
examples.solution:
\[\mathrm E(1/X)=\int_1^2\frac1x\frac{2x}3\,dx=\frac23,\qquad\mathrm E(1/X^2)=\frac23\int_1^2\frac1x\,dx=\frac{2\ln2}3.\]\[\operatorname{Var}(1/X)=\frac{2\ln2}3-\frac49.\]

The support stays above zero, so neither reciprocal has a singularity within the integration interval.

examples.title: 4 · No inverse is needed for an expectation
examples.question: X is uniform on \([0,2]\), and \(Y=(X-1)^2\). Find \(\mathrm E(Y)\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).
examples.solution:
\[\mathrm E(Y)=\frac12\int_0^2(x-1)^2\,dx=\frac13,\qquad\mathrm E(Y^2)=\frac12\int_0^2(x-1)^4\,dx=\frac15.\]\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac15-\frac19=\frac4{45}.\]

The function is not monotone on [0,2], but the direct expectation formula does not require monotonicity. In contrast, (E(X)−1)²=0 is not E(Y).

lessons.title: Increasing and decreasing transformations
lessons.summary: Transform the event and support before differentiating a new CDF.
lessons.objective: Derive complete CDFs and densities for monotone related variables, reversing inequalities when needed.
lessons.before: Complete CDFs and quantiles. Review inverse functions, the chain rule, logarithms and inequalities under decreasing functions.
lessons.ideas:
Begin with the event

Let Y=h(X) and write G(y)=P(Y≤y). First find the range of h on the support of X. Only then invert the inequality for interior y-values.

If h is increasing, \(h(X)\le y\) means \(X\le h^{-1}(y)\), so

\[G(y)=F_X(h^{-1}(y)).\]

If h is decreasing, the event becomes \(X\ge h^{-1}(y)\). For a variable with a density, the equality endpoint has no mass, so

\[G(y)=1-F_X(h^{-1}(y)).\]

Differentiate after stating the range

Give G=0 below the lower endpoint and G=1 at and above the upper endpoint. Differentiate the appropriate interior expression to obtain the density g. The chain-rule factor is essential; a substitution into f alone does not transform an area correctly.

As a check after the CDF derivation, \(g(y)=f_X(h^{-1}(y))|(h^{-1})'(y)|\) on a monotone branch. The absolute value makes a decreasing transformation's density non-negative. This is a check, not a replacement for the CDF argument required in the written questions.

Check endpoints and percentiles

Map both support endpoints, including limiting endpoints for an infinite original support. In a decreasing map, their order reverses. Solve G(q)=p for a transformed percentile; an increasing map transports the same percentile, whereas a decreasing map reverses cumulative probabilities.
lessons.method:
1. Find the transformed support and any mapped breakpoints.
  2. Write G(y)=P(h(X)≤y).
  3. Invert the event, reversing the inequality for a decreasing function.
  4. Insert the complete original CDF and state exterior values.
  5. Differentiate and check non-negativity and total mass.
mistakes: Substituting into a density omits the chain-rule factor.
A decreasing inverse requires a tail probability, not the original CDF value.
Transform the support as well as the formula.
The CDF must increase even when the transformation decreases.

examples.title: 1 · An affine change still needs a scale factor
examples.question: X has density \(6x(1-x)\) on \([0,1]\). Let \(Y=2X+1\). Find G and g.
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\- 2 \left(\frac{y}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} + 3 \left(\frac{y}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2},&1\le y\lt 3\\1,&y\ge 3.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\left(3 - y\right) \left(3 y - 3\right)}{4},&1\le y\le 3\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

For 1≤y≤3, Y≤y is X≤(y−1)/2. Integrating the original density gives F(x)=3x²−2x³. Substitute the inverse into F, then differentiate; the inverse contributes a factor 1/2. The resulting density integrates to 1.

examples.title: 2 · A nonlinear map can produce a constant density
examples.question: X has density \(\frac x4\) on \([1,3]\). Let \(Y=X^2+2\). Find G and g.
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 3\\\frac{y}{8} - \frac{3}{8},&3\le y\lt 11\\1,&y\ge 11.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{8},&3\le y\le 11\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The map is increasing on the entire support, with range [3,11]. For interior y, G(y)=F(√(y−2)). Since F(x)=(x²−1)/8, the substituted CDF is (y−3)/8. Differentiation gives 1/8; its area on [3,11] is 1.

examples.title: 3 · A reciprocal reverses the event
examples.question: X has density \(\frac{2x}{15}\) on \([1,4]\). Let \(Y=1/X\). Find G and g.
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt \frac{1}{4}\\\frac{16}{15} - \frac{1}{15 y^{2}},&\frac{1}{4}\le y\lt 1\\1,&y\ge 1.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{2}{15 y^{3}},&\frac{1}{4}\le y\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The support becomes [1/4,1]. For interior y, 1/X≤y is X≥1/y. Therefore G(y)=1−F(1/y), with F(x)=(x²−1)/15. Differentiating the tail expression gives a positive density; using F(1/y) alone would produce a decreasing function.

examples.title: 4 · A logarithm transforms the endpoints too
examples.question: X is uniform on \([1,5]\), and \(Y=\ln X\). Find the density of Y and \(\mathrm P(Y\le\ln3)\).
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\\frac{e^{y}}{4} - \frac{1}{4},&0\le y\lt \log{\left(5 \right)}\\1,&y\ge \log{\left(5 \right)}.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{e^{y}}{4},&0\le y\le \log{\left(5 \right)}\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The inverse is \(e^y\) and the range is [0,ln 5]. Thus \(G(y)=\mathrm P(X\le e^y)=(e^y-1)/4\) on that range. The required probability is \(G(\ln3)=(3-1)/4=1/2\).

lessons.title: Mapped breakpoints and multiple inverse branches
lessons.summary: Keep every contributing interval when a model or transformation changes formula.
lessons.objective: Derive piecewise transformed distributions from complete events and correctly mapped breakpoints.
lessons.before: Complete monotone transformations and piecewise CDFs. The two multi-branch examples extend the same CDF method; no joint densities are used.
lessons.ideas:
A breakpoint belongs to the variable being transformed

If the original density or CDF changes at x=c, then the corresponding transformed formula changes at y=h(c). For a monotone map, carry every original piece and any support gap through the inverse in the correct order.

Do not restart the accumulated mass

A transformed CDF must join continuously across its interior breakpoints. Its density may jump. Test each CDF branch at both adjacent boundaries, and check that the final branch reaches 1. A gap remains a flat section of the CDF, rather than a new atom.

For a non-monotone map, invert the whole event

An inverse may have more than one branch. For Y=X² and y≥0,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(-\sqrt y\le X\le\sqrt y).\]

Intersect that interval with the actual support. If a boundary crosses a support endpoint, the contributing intervals change. Similarly, |X−c|≤y describes an interval [c−y,c+y], not one inverse point. Form its probability first, then differentiate each resulting y-branch.

Endpoint singularities can be integrable

A transformed density may become unbounded near an endpoint while retaining finite area 1. Check its improper integral; a large or infinite limiting height is not a point mass. Assigning a density value at the single endpoint does not change the CDF.
lessons.method:
1. Map every original endpoint and breakpoint.
  2. For each y-range, solve the full event h(X)≤y.
  3. Intersect with all original support pieces.
  4. Calculate the cumulative probability, retaining earlier mass.
  5. Check joins, differentiate by branch, and verify total mass.
mistakes: A transformed breakpoint is h(c), not c.
A square root used as an inverse may hide a second preimage.
The lower and upper branches may contribute together.
A density singularity is not an atom if its area remains finite.

examples.title: 1 · Move the join with the transformation
examples.question: The density is \(\frac14\) on \([0,2)\), \(\frac{4-x}{4}\) on \([2,4]\), and zero elsewhere. For \(Y=\sqrt{X+1}\), find G and g.
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\\frac{y^{2}}{4} - \frac{1}{4},&1\le y\lt \sqrt{3}\\1 - \frac{\left(5 - y^{2}\right)^{2}}{8},&\sqrt{3}\le y\lt \sqrt{5}\\1,&y\ge \sqrt{5}.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{y}{2},&1\le y\lt \sqrt{3}\\\frac{y \left(5 - y^{2}\right)}{2},&\sqrt{3}\le y\le \sqrt{5}\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The range is [1,√5], and x=2 maps to y=√3. The inverse event is X≤y²−1. Substitute into the correct CDF branch: F(x)=x/4 before 2 and F(x)=1−(4−x)²/8 afterwards. Both transformed branches give 1/2 at √3.

examples.title: 2 · A square includes both signs
examples.question: A density is \(\frac{2(x+1)}3\) on \([-1,0)\), \(\frac{4(1-x)}3\) on \([0,1]\), and zero elsewhere. Find the distribution of \(Y=X^2\).
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\2 \sqrt{y} - y,&0\le y\lt 1\\1,&y\ge 1.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}-1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{y}},&0\lt y\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

For \(0\le y\le1\), integrate from \(-\sqrt y\) to \(\sqrt y\), splitting at 0. The left and right contributions sum to \(2\sqrt y-y\). Differentiating gives \(y^{-1/2}-1\) on (0,1). Its improper integral is \([2\sqrt y-y]_0^1=1\). The infinite limiting height near 0 creates no atom because G is continuous there; its value at that single endpoint may be assigned arbitrarily.

examples.title: 3 · A decreasing map preserves a gap
examples.question: A density is \(\frac12\) on \([0,1]\) and \([2,3]\), zero elsewhere. Let \(Y=4-X\). Find its CDF.
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\\frac{y}{2} - \frac{1}{2},&1\le y\lt 2\\\frac{1}{2},&2\le y\lt 3\\\frac{y}{2} - 1,&3\le y\lt 4\\1,&y\ge 4.\end{cases}\]

The transformed support is [1,2] together with [3,4]. The event X≥4−y uses the original upper tail. Between y=2 and y=3 the CDF stays at 1/2 because no transformed values lie in that gap. Both joins are continuous; the density is zero on the gap.

examples.title: 4 · The number of inverse branches can change
examples.question: X is uniform on \([0,3]\), and \(Y=|X-1|\). Find G, g and \(\mathrm P(Y\le\frac32)\).
examples.solution:
\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\\frac{2 y}{3},&0\le y\lt 1\\\frac{y}{3} + \frac{1}{3},&1\le y\lt 2\\1,&y\ge 2.\end{cases}\]\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{2}{3},&0\le y\lt 1\\\frac{1}{3},&1\le y\le 2\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The event is 1−y≤X≤1+y, clipped to [0,3]. For 0≤y<1 its length is 2y. For 1≤y≤2 it runs from 0 to 1+y, with length 1+y. Divide each by 3. The CDF joins at 2/3, and G(3/2)=5/6.

questions.answer_html: Normalising constant k: \(\frac{1}{4}\); Interval probability: \(\frac{1}{2}\); Single-point probability: \(0\)
questions.solution_html: Integrate the density over its whole support to find k. The central half-interval has half the area for this affine density. A single point has zero probability.

questions.answer_html: Normalising constant k: \(\frac{2}{5}\); Interval probability: \(\frac{1}{2}\); Single-point probability: \(0\)
questions.solution_html: Integrate the density over its whole support to find k. The central half-interval has half the area for this affine density. A single point has zero probability.

questions.title: Both coefficients of a piecewise density
questions.prompt_html: A density equals ax on \([0,1)\), b on \([1,3]\), and zero elsewhere. Given \(\mathrm P(X\lt1)=\frac{1}{4}\), find a and b. No density-matching condition is imposed.
questions.answer_html: Coefficient a: \(\frac{1}{2}\); Coefficient b: \(\frac{3}{8}\)
questions.solution_html: Use the stated first-piece area to find a, then use total probability 1 to find b.
questions.hint_html: Write the support first. Distinguish a density height from cumulative probability and include every requested branch or coefficient.

questions.prompt_html: A density equals ax on \([0,2)\), b on \([2,4]\), and zero elsewhere. Given \(\mathrm P(X\lt2)=\frac{2}{5}\), find a and b. No density-matching condition is imposed.
questions.answer_html: Coefficient a: \(\frac{1}{5}\); Coefficient b: \(\frac{3}{10}\)
questions.solution_html: Use the stated first-piece area to find a, then use total probability 1 to find b.
questions.hint_html: Write the support first. Distinguish a density height from cumulative probability and include every requested branch or coefficient.

questions.title: Keep a gap empty
questions.prompt_html: A density equals c on \([0,1]\) and \([2,4]\), and is zero elsewhere. Give c, the density in the gap, and \(\mathrm P(\frac{1}{2}\lt X\lt3)\).
questions.answer_html: Height c: \(\frac{1}{3}\); Density in the gap: \(0\); Cross-gap probability: \(\frac{1}{2}\)
questions.solution_html: Normalise using the combined lengths of the two support intervals. The event receives no contribution from the gap.
questions.hint_html: Write the support first. Distinguish a density height from cumulative probability and include every requested branch or coefficient.

questions.title: Calibrating a service-life model
questions.prompt_html:
The service life \(T\), in hours, of a sensor is modelled by

\[F(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\lt0,\\1-e^{-\lambda t},&t\ge0,\end{cases}\]

where \(\lambda\gt0\). Tests indicate that \(\mathrm P(T\gt240)=\frac13\).

  1. Find \(\lambda\), and hence give the probability density function of \(T\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(120\lt T\le360)\), giving an exact answer.

    [2]

  3. Find the median service life in exact form.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\lambda=\frac{\ln3}{240},\qquad f(t)=\frac{\ln3}{240}e^{-t\ln3/240}\quad(t\ge0),\]

\(f(t)=0\) for \(t\lt0\).

(b)

\[\mathrm P(120\lt T\le360)=\frac{2\sqrt3}{9}.\]

(c)

\[m=\frac{240\ln2}{\ln3}\text{ hours}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The given survival probability gives \(1-F(240)=e^{-240\lambda}=1/3\). Taking natural logarithms gives

\[-240\lambda=-\ln3,\qquad\lambda=\frac{\ln3}{240}.\]

Differentiate the CDF on its non-constant branch:

\[f(t)=F'(t)=\frac{\ln3}{240}e^{-t\ln3/240},\qquad t\ge0.\]

Set \(f(t)=0\) for \(t\lt0\). This density is non-negative and its integral on \([0,\infty)\) is 1.

(b)

Subtract CDF values, keeping the tail signs in the correct order:

\[F(360)-F(120)=e^{-120\lambda}-e^{-360\lambda}=3^{-1/2}-3^{-3/2}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{9}.\]

The inclusion of a single endpoint does not change a probability for this continuous distribution.

(c)

At the median \(F(m)=1/2\). Thus \(e^{-\lambda m}=1/2\), so

\[m=\frac{\ln2}{\lambda}=\frac{240\ln2}{\ln3}.\]

This value lies in the support \(m\ge0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(1-F(240)\), not \(F(240)\), before differentiating.

(b)

Write the probability as the difference of two survival probabilities.

(c)

Solve \(F(m)=1/2\).

questions.title: Independent protective seals
questions.prompt_html:
The time \(T\), in days, until a protective seal fails has CDF

\[F(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\lt0,\\1-e^{-bt},&t\ge0,\end{cases}\]

where \(b\gt0\). The probability that one seal fails within 60 days is \(3/5\).

  1. Find \(b\) exactly.

    [1]

  2. Find the probability that one seal has failed by day 120.

    [2]

  3. A unit contains \(n\) seals whose failure times are independent. Find the least integer \(n\) for which the probability that at least one seal is still functioning on day 120 is greater than \(0.99\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[b=\frac{\ln(5/2)}{60}.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(T\le120)=\frac{21}{25}.\]

(c)

\[n=27.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The condition \(F(60)=3/5\) gives \(e^{-60b}=2/5\). Taking logarithms,

\[b=-\frac1{60}\ln\frac25=\frac{\ln(5/2)}{60}.\]

(b)

Since \(e^{-60b}=2/5\),

\[F(120)=1-(e^{-60b})^2=1-\left(\frac25\right)^2=\frac{21}{25}.\]

(c)

All \(n\) seals have failed by day 120 with probability \((21/25)^n\). Therefore

\[1-\left(\frac{21}{25}\right)^n\gt0.99 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \left(\frac{21}{25}\right)^n\lt0.01.\]

Because \(\ln(21/25)\lt0\), division reverses the inequality:

\[n\gt\frac{\ln0.01}{\ln(21/25)}=26.41285\ldots.\]

Thus the least integer is \(27\). At \(n=26\) the required probability is \(0.989254\); at \(n=27\) it is \(0.990973\), confirming the strict boundary.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Substitute 60 into the CDF.

(b)

Day 120 is twice day 60, so square the survival probability.

(c)

Use the complement of all seals having failed; do not round the one-seal probability.

\[F(t)=\begin{cases}0,&t\lt2,\\1-e^{-(t-2)/6},&t\ge2.\end{cases}\]

  1. Write down the probability density function of \(T\).

    [1]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(5\lt T\lt11)\), giving an exact answer.

    [2]

  3. Find the 90th percentile of \(T\), in exact form.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[f(t)=\begin{cases}\frac16e^{-(t-2)/6},&t\ge2,\\0,&t\lt2.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[e^{-1/2}-e^{-3/2}.\]

(c)

\[2+6\ln10\text{ minutes}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the non-constant branch of \(F\). The lower endpoint is 2, not 0:

\[f(t)=\frac16e^{-(t-2)/6}\quad(t\ge2),\qquad f(t)=0\quad(t\lt2).\]

(b)

Use the CDF difference:

\[F(11)-F(5)=(1-e^{-9/6})-(1-e^{-3/6})=e^{-1/2}-e^{-3/2}.\]

(c)

Let the percentile be \(q\). The equation is

\[1-e^{-(q-2)/6}=0.9.\]

Then \(e^{-(q-2)/6}=0.1\), so \(-(q-2)/6=-\ln10\). Consequently

\[q=2+6\ln10.\]

This is greater than the lower endpoint 2, as required.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The support starts at 2 minutes.

(b)

Subtract the CDF values at 5 and 11.

(c)

The 90th percentile leaves 10% in the upper tail.

questions.title: Matching two pieces of a density
questions.prompt_html:
A continuous random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}mx,&0\le x\lt1,\\\frac{k}{x^2}+c,&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density itself is continuous at \(x=1\), and \(\mathrm P(X\le1)=3/8\).

  1. Find \(m\), \(k\) and \(c\).

    [4]

  2. Find the exact interquartile range of \(X\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[m=\frac34,\qquad k=\frac{21}{32},\qquad c=\frac3{32}.\]

(b)

\[2\sqrt2-1-\frac{\sqrt6}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The probability to the left of 1 gives

\[\int_0^1mx\,dx=\frac m2=\frac38,\qquad m=\frac34.\]

The stated continuity condition gives \(k+c=3/4\). The remaining probability is \(5/8\), so

\[\int_1^3\left(\frac{k}{x^2}+c\right)dx=\frac{2k}{3}+2c=\frac58.\]

Subtract the latter equation from twice the continuity equation: \(4k/3=7/8\). Hence

\[k=\frac{21}{32},\qquad c=\frac3{32}.\]

Both pieces are non-negative on their stated intervals.

(b)

Since \(F(1)=3/8\), the lower quartile is in the first branch and the upper quartile is in the second.

\[\frac{3Q_1^2}{8}=\frac14,\qquad Q_1=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}.\]

For \(1\le x\le3\), accumulate the probability from the first branch:

\[F(x)=\frac38+\int_1^x\left(\frac{21}{32u^2}+\frac3{32}\right)du =\frac{30+3x-21/x}{32}.\]

Setting \(F(Q_3)=3/4\) gives \(3Q_3-21/Q_3=-6\), or

\[Q_3^2+2Q_3-7=0.\]

The admissible root is \(Q_3=2\sqrt2-1\); the other root is outside \([1,3]\). Therefore

\[\mathrm{IQR}=2\sqrt2-1-\frac{\sqrt6}{3}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the given probability, the total integral and the explicitly stated continuity.

(b)

Locate each quartile before selecting a formula. Include the probability already accumulated at 1.

questions.title: Two linear sections
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}k(2+x),&0\le x\lt1,\\k(4-x),&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\]

where \(k\) is a positive constant.

  1. Find \(k\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact interquartile range.

    [4]

  3. Find \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\) exactly.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[k=\frac2{13}.\]

(b)

\[6-\frac{\sqrt{17}+\sqrt{29}}2\]

(c)

\[\frac{145}{234}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Normalisation gives

\[1=k\int_0^1(2+x)dx+k\int_1^3(4-x)dx=k\left(\frac52+4\right)=\frac{13k}{2}.\]

Hence \(k=2/13\). Both linear factors are positive on the specified intervals.

(b)

The CDF on the support is

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}(x^2+4x)/13,&0\le x\lt1,\\(8x-x^2-2)/13,&1\le x\le3.\end{cases}\]

Because \(F(1)=5/13\), the lower quartile is below 1 and the upper quartile is above 1.

\[Q_1^2+4Q_1=\frac{13}4,\qquad Q_1=-2 + \frac{\sqrt{29}}{2}.\]
\[8Q_3-Q_3^2-2=\frac{39}4,\qquad Q_3=4 - \frac{\sqrt{17}}{2}.\]

In each quadratic, discard the root outside the relevant interval. Thus

\[\mathrm{IQR}=6-\frac{\sqrt{17}+\sqrt{29}}2.\]

(c)

Compute both moments, integrating over both pieces:

\[\mathrm E(X)=\frac2{13}\left[\int_0^1x(2+x)dx+\int_1^3x(4-x)dx\right]=\frac{4}{3}.\]
\[\mathrm E(X^2)=\frac2{13}\left[\int_0^1x^2(2+x)dx+\int_1^3x^2(4-x)dx\right]=\frac{187}{78}.\]

Therefore

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{187}{78}-\left(\frac{4}{3}\right)^2=\frac{145}{234}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The areas from both intervals must total 1.

(b)

Find \(F(1)\) to decide which branch contains each quartile.

(c)

Use \(\mathrm E(X^2)-[\mathrm E(X)]^2\), not the difference of the two integrals.

marking_criteria.description_html: Set up and evaluate the second moment.

questions.title: An inverse-square contribution
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac16\left(2+\frac3{x^2}\right),&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\), including values outside the support.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact interquartile range.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac16\left(2x-\frac3x+1\right),&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[\frac{- \sqrt{97} + 6 + \sqrt{145}}{8}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(1\le x\le3\), integrate from the actual lower endpoint:

\[F(x)=\int_1^x\left(\frac13+\frac1{2u^2}\right)du =\left[\frac u3-\frac1{2u}\right]_1^x =\frac{2x-3/x+1}{6}.\]

The values at the endpoints are 0 and 1, so the complete CDF is

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac16\left(2x-\frac3x+1\right),&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}.\]

(b)

For a percentile probability \(p\), the equation \(F(q)=p\) is

\[2q^2+(1-6p)q-3=0.\]

At \(p=1/4\), this becomes \(4q^2-q-6=0\), so

\[Q_1=\frac{1 + \sqrt{97}}{8}.\]

At \(p=3/4\), this becomes \(4q^2-7q-6=0\), so

\[Q_3=\frac{7 + \sqrt{145}}{8}.\]

In both cases choose the positive root in \([1,3]\). Subtraction gives

\[\mathrm{IQR}=\frac{- \sqrt{97} + 6 + \sqrt{145}}{8}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The lower endpoint is 1; the integration constant is not zero.

(b)

Multiply a quartile equation by \(6q\), then check the root lies between 1 and 3.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the correct expression inside the support.

questions.title: A conditional tail probability
questions.prompt_html:
The density of a random variable \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}3e^{-3(x-1)},&x\ge1,\\0,&x\lt1.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(X\gt2\mid X\gt3/2)\).

    [2]

  3. Find the exact median of \(X\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\1 - e^{3 - 3 x},&1\le x.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[e^{-3/2}.\]

(c)

\[1+\frac{\ln2}{3}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(x\ge1\),

\[F(x)=\int_1^x3e^{-3(u-1)}du=\left[-e^{-3(u-1)}\right]_1^x=1-e^{-3(x-1)}.\]

For \(x\lt1\), \(F(x)=0\). The CDF is continuous at 1 and tends to 1 as \(x\to\infty\).

(b)

The event \(X\gt2\) is contained in \(X\gt3/2\), so

\[\mathrm P(X\gt2\mid X\gt3/2) =\frac{1-F(2)}{1-F(3/2)} =\frac{e^{-3}}{e^{-3/2}}=e^{-3/2}.\]

This is obtained directly from conditional probability; no special distribution property is needed.

(c)

Set \(F(m)=1/2\). Then \(e^{-3(m-1)}=1/2\), giving

\[m=1+\frac{\ln2}{3}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower endpoint 1.

(b)

Use the ratio of the two upper-tail probabilities.

(c)

Retain the shift by 1 when taking logarithms.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give the correct lower branch and support.

questions.title: A quadratic exponent in a CDF
questions.prompt_html:
The cumulative distribution function of \(X\) is

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt0,\\1-e^{-x^2/9},&x\ge0.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find \(\mathrm P(X\gt3\sqrt2)\) exactly.

    [2]

  2. Find the exact interquartile range of \(X\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[e^{-2}.\]

(b)

\[3\left(\sqrt{\ln4}-\sqrt{\ln(4/3)}\right).\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the upper tail:

\[\mathrm P(X\gt3\sqrt2)=1-F(3\sqrt2)=e^{-(3\sqrt2)^2/9}=e^{-2}.\]

(b)

At the lower quartile,

\[1-e^{-Q_1^2/9}=\frac14 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_1^2=9\ln\frac43.\]

At the upper quartile,

\[1-e^{-Q_3^2/9}=\frac34 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q_3^2=9\ln4.\]

Both quartiles are non-negative. Hence

\[Q_1=3\sqrt{\ln(4/3)},\qquad Q_3=3\sqrt{\ln4},\]

and

\[\mathrm{IQR}=3\left(\sqrt{\ln4}-\sqrt{\ln(4/3)}\right).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use \(1-F\), and square the entire argument.

(b)

After taking logarithms, choose non-negative square roots.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the lower quartile with the correct sign.

questions.title: Recovering a piecewise CDF
questions.prompt_html:
The continuous random variable \(X\) has CDF

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt2,\\\frac{x+a}{6},&2\le x\lt5,\\\frac{x^2+b}{112},&5\le x\lt9,\\1,&x\ge9,\end{cases}\]

where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants.

  1. Find \(a\) and \(b\), and check continuity at \(x=5\).

    [2]

  2. Find the probability density function of \(X\).

    [2]

  3. Given that \(\mathrm E(X)=\frac{449}{84}\), find \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

    [3]

  4. Find the 10th and 90th percentiles of \(X\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=-2,\qquad b=31,\qquad F(5)=\frac12.\]

(b)

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{6},&2\le x\lt 5\\\frac{x}{56},&5\le x\le 9\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(c)

\[\frac{31247}{7056}\]

(d)

\[q_{0.1}=\frac{13}{5},\qquad q_{0.9}=\frac{\sqrt{1745}}{5}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Continuity at the endpoints gives \((2+a)/6=0\) and \((81+b)/112=1\). Hence \(a=-2\) and \(b=31\). At the interior join,

\[\frac{5-2}{6}=\frac12=\frac{25+31}{112}.\]

Thus the three continuity requirements are consistent.

(b)

Differentiate the two non-constant CDF branches:

\[\frac d{dx}\frac{x-2}6=\frac16,\qquad \frac d{dx}\frac{x^2+31}{112}=\fracx{56}.\]

Thus

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{6},&2\le x\lt 5\\\frac{x}{56},&5\le x\le 9\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}.\]

The density need not be continuous at 5; it is the CDF that must be continuous for this continuous distribution.

(c)

The second moment is

\[\mathrm E(X^2)=\int_2^5\frac{x^2}6\,dx+\int_5^9\frac{x^3}{56}\,dx =\left[\frac{x^3}{18}\right]_2^5+\left[\frac{x^4}{224}\right]_5^9=33.\]

Use the supplied mean:

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=33-\left(\frac{449}{84}\right)^2=\frac{31247}{7056}.\]

(d)

The joining probability is \(1/2\), so the 10th percentile lies in \([2,5]\) and the 90th lies in \([5,9]\).

\[\frac{q_{0.1}-2}6=\frac1{10}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_{0.1}=\frac{13}{5}.\]
\[\frac{q_{0.9}^2+31}{112}=\frac9{10} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q_{0.9}=\frac{\sqrt{1745}}{5}.\]

The negative square root is excluded by the support.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the CDF values 0 and 1 at the two endpoints, then check the join.

(b)

Differentiate only on the interiors of the pieces.

(c)

Calculate the second moment, then subtract the square of the given mean.

(d)

Compare each percentile probability with \(F(5)\).

questions.title: An asymmetric triangular density
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has CDF

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt-2,\\\frac{(x+2)^2}{24},&-2\le x\lt1,\\1-\frac{(6-x)^2}{40},&1\le x\lt6,\\1,&x\ge6.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the density of \(X\) and sketch its graph, labelling the endpoints and the maximum.

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

    [3]

  3. Find the exact interquartile range.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{x + 2}{12},&-2\le x\lt 1\\\frac{6 - x}{20},&1\le x\le 6\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The graph is the triangle with vertices \((-2,0),(1,1/4),(6,0)\).

(b)

\[\frac{5}{3}\]

(c)

\[8-\sqrt6-\sqrt{10}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiating the CDF gives

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{x + 2}{12},&-2\le x\lt 1\\\frac{6 - x}{20},&1\le x\le 6\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}.\]

At the join, both linear branches have value \(1/4\). The density increases linearly from \((-2,0)\) to \((1,1/4)\), then decreases linearly to \((6,0)\). It is zero outside \([-2,6]\). Its total triangular area is \(\tfrac12(8)(1/4)=1\).

(b)

Use the first-moment integral, including the negative part of the support:

\[\mathrm E(X)=\int_{-2}^1\frac{x(x+2)}{12}dx+\int_1^6\frac{x(6-x)}{20}dx.\]
\[=\left[\frac{x^3}{36}+\frac{x^2}{12}\right]_{-2}^1+ \left[\frac{3x^2}{20}-\frac{x^3}{60}\right]_1^6=\frac{5}{3}.\]

A density is non-negative, but contributions to \(\mathrm E(X)\) may be negative when \(x\lt0\).

(c)

Since \(F(1)=3/8\), use the left branch for \(Q_1\) and the right branch for \(Q_3\):

\[\frac{(Q_1+2)^2}{24}=\frac14,\qquad Q_1=-2+\sqrt6.\]
\[1-\frac{(6-Q_3)^2}{40}=\frac34,\qquad Q_3=6-\sqrt{10}.\]

The signs are selected using \(-2\le Q_1\le1\) and \(1\le Q_3\le6\). Hence

\[\mathrm{IQR}=8-\sqrt6-\sqrt{10}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate each branch and evaluate the heights at \(-2,1,6\).

(b)

Use \(\int xf(x)\,dx\), not the area under the density.

(c)

The median and the two quartiles need not lie in the same branch.

marking_criteria.description_html: Label the three vertices and zero density outside the support.

questions.title: A quartile determines a cubic density
questions.prompt_html:
A random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}ax-bx^3,&0\le x\lt2,\\c,&2\le x\le4,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is continuous at \(x=2\), and the upper quartile of \(X\) is 2.

  1. Find \(a,b,c\).

    [4]

  2. Find the exact median of \(X\).

    [3]

  3. Find \(\mathrm E(\sqrt X)\), giving your answer correct to 2 decimal places.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=\frac{11}{16},\qquad b=\frac5{32},\qquad c=\frac18.\]

(b)

\[\sqrt{\frac{22-2\sqrt{41}}5}\]

(c)

\[\mathrm E(\sqrt X)=\frac{17 \sqrt{2} + 30}{45}\approx1.20.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The probability in \([2,4]\) is \(1/4\), so \(2c=1/4\) and \(c=1/8\). The first branch has mass \(3/4\):

\[\int_0^2(ax-bx^3)dx=2a-4b=\frac34.\]

Continuity gives \(2a-8b=1/8\). Subtracting yields \(4b=5/8\), and hence

\[b=\frac5{32},\qquad a=\frac{11}{16}.\]

The first density is \(x(22-5x^2)/32\). On \([0,2]\), both factors are non-negative, so this is a valid density.

(b)

Since \(F(2)=3/4\), the median is in the cubic-density section. Its CDF there is

\[F(x)=\frac{11x^2}{32}-\frac{5x^4}{128}.\]

Set \(F(m)=1/2\), giving \(5m^4-44m^2+64=0\). With \(z=m^2\),

\[5z^2-44z+64=0,\qquad z=\frac{22\pm2\sqrt{41}}5.\]

The plus sign gives \(z\gt4\), which is outside this branch. Therefore

\[m=\sqrt{\frac{22-2\sqrt{41}}5}.\]

(c)

Use \(g(x)=\sqrt x\) in the expectation integral:

\[\mathrm E(\sqrt X)=\int_0^2\left(\frac{11}{16}x^{3/2}-\frac5{32}x^{7/2}\right)dx+\frac18\int_2^4x^{1/2}dx.\]
\[=\left[\frac{11}{40}x^{5/2}-\frac5{144}x^{9/2}\right]_0^2+ \left[\frac1{12}x^{3/2}\right]_2^4=\frac{17 \sqrt{2} + 30}{45}.\]

Thus the required value is \(1.20\) to 2 decimal places. This is not generally \(\sqrt{\mathrm E(X)}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The upper-quartile condition fixes the mass of the constant section. Continuity is an additional stated condition.

(b)

Put \(z=m^2\), and use \(0\lt m\lt2\) to choose the root.

(c)

Multiply each density branch by \(\sqrt x\) before integrating.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use continuity to form a second linear equation.
Set the integrated first branch equal to one half.
Solve the quadratic in the squared median.
Choose the correct root and square root.
Give the requested rounded value from unrounded calculations.

questions.title: A curved section followed by a line
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}kx(3-x),&0\le x\lt1,\\k(3-x),&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find \(k\).

    [2]

  2. Given that \(\mathrm E(X)=\frac{49}{38}\), find \(\operatorname{Var}(X)\).

    [3]

  3. Find the exact median.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[k=\frac6{19}.\]

(b)

\[\frac{2929}{7220}\]

(c)

\[3-\sqrt{\frac{19}{6}}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Both pieces are non-negative. Their total mass must be 1:

\[k\left[\frac{3x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1+k\left[3x-\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^3 =k\left(\frac76+2\right)=1.\]

Thus \(k=6/19\).

(b)

The second moment is

\[\mathrm E(X^2)=\frac6{19}\left(\int_0^1x^3(3-x)dx+\int_1^3x^2(3-x)dx\right)=\frac{393}{190}.\]

Using the given mean,

\[\operatorname{Var}(X)=\frac{393}{190}-\left(\frac{49}{38}\right)^2=\frac{2929}{7220}.\]

(c)

First, \(F(1)=\frac6{19}\cdot\frac76=\frac7{19}\lt1/2\), so the median is above 1. Use the right-hand tail:

\[\mathrm P(X\gt m)=\int_m^3\frac6{19}(3-x)dx=\frac3{19}(3-m)^2.\]

At the median this is \(1/2\). Therefore

\[(3-m)^2=\frac{19}{6},\qquad m=3-\sqrt{\frac{19}{6}}.\]

The other algebraic root is greater than the upper support endpoint.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate the two sections separately.

(b)

questions.title: Fractional moments and a fourth root
questions.prompt_html:
The cumulative distribution function of \(X\) is

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt0,\\x^3/64,&0\le x\lt4,\\1,&x\ge4.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find \(\mathrm E(\sqrt X)\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)\).

    [2]

  3. The variable \(Y\) is defined by \(Y=X^{1/4}\). Find its density.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{12}{7}.\]

(b)

\[\frac3{49}.\]

(c)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{3 y^{11}}{16},&0\le y\le \sqrt{2}\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The density is \(f(x)=3x^2/64\) for \(0\le x\le4\). Therefore

\[\mathrm E(\sqrt X)=\int_0^4\sqrt x\,\frac{3x^2}{64}dx =\frac3{64}\left[\frac27x^{7/2}\right]_0^4=\frac{12}{7}.\]

(b)

The second moment of \(\sqrt X\) is \(\mathrm E(X)\), not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\):

\[\mathrm E(X)=\frac3{64}\int_0^4x^3dx=3.\]

Thus

\[\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)=3-\left(\frac{12}{7}\right)^2=\frac3{49}.\]

(c)

The transformation \(Y=\sqrt[4]{X}\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(0\le Y\le\sqrt{2}\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\ley^{4})=F(y^{4}).\]

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\\frac{y^{12}}{64},&0\le y\lt \sqrt{2}\\1,&y\ge \sqrt{2}.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{3 y^{11}}{16},&0\le y\le \sqrt{2}\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate the CDF before calculating the moment.

(b)

Use \((\sqrt X)^2=X\).

(c)

For \(y\ge0\), \(Y\le y\) is equivalent to \(X\le y^4\).

questions.title: A square of a variable with negative values
questions.prompt_html:
A continuous random variable \(X\) has CDF

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt-2,\\(x+2)^2/6,&-2\le x\lt0,\\1-(1-x)^2/3,&0\le x\lt1,\\1,&x\ge1.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the density of \(X\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(-1\le X\le1/2)\).

    [2]

  3. Find \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

    [2]

  4. Find \(\operatorname{Var}(X^2)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{x + 2}{3},&-2\le x\lt 0\\\frac{2 \left(1 - x\right)}{3},&0\le x\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[\frac34.\]

(c)

\[\frac{1}{2}\]

(d)

\[\frac{29}{60}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Differentiate the two non-constant branches. This gives

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{x + 2}{3},&-2\le x\lt 0\\\frac{2 \left(1 - x\right)}{3},&0\le x\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}.\]

At the join the CDF has value \(2/3\) from both sides.

(b)

The interval crosses the join, so use CDF values from different branches:

\[F(1/2)-F(-1)=\left(1-\frac{(1-1/2)^2}{3}\right)-\frac{(-1+2)^2}{6} =\frac{11}{12}-\frac16=\frac34.\]

(c)

Integrate against the density:

\[\mathrm E(X^2)=\frac13\int_{-2}^0x^2(x+2)dx+\frac23\int_0^1x^2(1-x)dx=\frac{1}{2}.\]

(d)

The second moment of \(X^2\) is \(\mathrm E(X^4)\):

\[\mathrm E(X^4)=\frac13\int_{-2}^0x^4(x+2)dx+\frac23\int_0^1x^4(1-x)dx=\frac{11}{15}.\]

Hence

\[\operatorname{Var}(X^2)=\frac{11}{15}-\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^2=\frac{29}{60}.\]

This is not \([\operatorname{Var}(X)]^2\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Differentiate piecewise, keeping the original support.

(b)

The CDF automatically includes probability across the join.

(c)

Negative values of x still contribute positively to this moment.

(d)

Use \(\mathrm E(X^4)-[\mathrm E(X^2)]^2\).

questions.title: A density with a permitted jump
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}a+x/6,&0\le x\lt2,\\2a-x/12,&2\le x\le4,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\]

where \(a\) is a constant. The density is not required to be continuous at \(x=2\).

  1. Find \(a\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

    [3]

  3. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=\frac7{36}.\]

(b)

\[\frac{31}{9}\]

(c)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x \left(3 x + 7\right)}{36},&0\le x\lt 2\\\frac{- 3 x^{2} + 28 x + 8}{72},&2\le x\lt 4\\1,&x\ge 4.\end{cases}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Normalisation, not a continuity condition, determines \(a\):

\[\int_0^2\left(a+\frac x6\right)dx+\int_2^4\left(2a-\frac x{12}\right)dx =\left(2a+\frac13\right)+\left(4a-\frac12\right)=1.\]

Thus \(6a=7/6\) and \(a=7/36\). Both pieces remain non-negative on their intervals; the smallest value in the second piece is \(1/18\).

(b)

Multiply by \(x^2\) on both intervals:

\[\mathrm E(X^2)=\int_0^2x^2\left(\frac7{36}+\frac x6\right)dx+ \int_2^4x^2\left(\frac7{18}-\frac x{12}\right)dx.\]
\[=\left[\frac{7x^3}{108}+\frac{x^4}{24}\right]_0^2+ \left[\frac{7x^3}{54}-\frac{x^4}{48}\right]_2^4=\frac{31}{9}.\]

(c)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(0\le x\lt 2\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{6 u + 7}{36}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u \left(3 u + 7\right)}{36}\right]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x \left(3 x + 7\right)}{36}\]

Include the accumulated probability \(\frac{13}{18}\) from the earlier interval for \(2\le x\lt 4\):

\[F(x)=\frac{13}{18}+\int_{2}^{x}\frac{14 - 3 u}{36}\,du=\frac{13}{18}+\left[\frac{u \left(28 - 3 u\right)}{72}\right]_{2}^{x}=\frac{- 3 x^{2} + 28 x + 8}{72}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x \left(3 x + 7\right)}{36},&0\le x\lt 2\\\frac{- 3 x^{2} + 28 x + 8}{72},&2\le x\lt 4\\1,&x\ge 4.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Do not set the two density values equal at 2.

(b)

Each density section contributes to the second moment.

(c)

The second branch must include \(F(2)\), even though the density jumps there.

questions.title: Accumulation across a triangular model
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}x/12,&0\le x\lt3,\\(8-x)/20,&3\le x\le8,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function.

    [3]

  2. Find the exact median.

    [2]

  3. Find \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

    [2]

  4. Find \(\mathrm P(2\le X\le5)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{2}}{24},&0\le x\lt 3\\1-\frac{(8-x)^2}{40},&3\le x\lt 8\\1,&x\ge 8.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[8-2\sqrt5\]

(c)

\[\frac{97}{6}\]

(d)

\[\frac{73}{120}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(0\le x\lt 3\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{u}{12}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u^{2}}{24}\right]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{2}}{24}\]

Include the accumulated probability \(\frac{3}{8}\) from the earlier interval for \(3\le x\lt 8\):

\[F(x)=\frac{3}{8}+\int_{3}^{x}\frac{8 - u}{20}\,du=\frac{3}{8}+\left[\frac{u \left(16 - u\right)}{40}\right]_{3}^{x}=1-\frac{(8-x)^2}{40}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{2}}{24},&0\le x\lt 3\\1-\frac{(8-x)^2}{40},&3\le x\lt 8\\1,&x\ge 8.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(b)

Since \(F(3)=3/8\lt1/2\), the median lies between 3 and 8. Thus

\[1-\frac{(8-m)^2}{40}=\frac12,\quad (8-m)^2=20.\]

Select the root inside the support:

\[m=8-2\sqrt5.\]

(c)

Using both intervals,

\[\mathrm E(X^2)=\int_0^3\frac{x^3}{12}dx+\int_3^8\frac{x^2(8-x)}{20}dx =\left[\frac{x^4}{48}\right]_0^3+\left[\frac{2x^3}{15}-\frac{x^4}{80}\right]_3^8=\frac{97}{6}.\]

(d)

The lower limit is in the increasing section and the upper limit in the decreasing section:

\[F(5)-F(2)=1-\frac9{40}-\frac4{24}=\frac{73}{120}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Check the accumulated probability at 3 before integrating the second piece.

(b)

Use the descending section, whose total right tail is particularly simple.

(c)

Integrate \(x^2f(x)\).

(d)

Use a CDF difference across the join.

Give a complete CDF with correct endpoints.

questions.title: A quadratic rise and a linear fall
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}kx^2,&0\le x\lt2,\\k(6-x),&2\le x\le6,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\]

where \(k\gt0\).

  1. Sketch the density, labelling its maximum in terms of \(k\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(k\).

    [2]

  3. Find the cumulative distribution function.

    [3]

  4. Find the exact median.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The curve rises quadratically from \((0,0)\) to \((2,4k)\), then falls linearly to \((6,0)\).

(b)

\[k=\frac3{32}.\]

(c)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{3}}{32},&0\le x\lt 2\\1-\frac{3(6-x)^2}{64},&2\le x\lt 6\\1,&x\ge 6.\end{cases}\]

(d)

\[6-\frac{4\sqrt6}{3}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The first branch is an upward-curving quadratic for \(0\le x\lt2\). Its limiting height at 2 is \(4k\). The second branch starts at the same height and decreases linearly to zero at 6. The density is zero elsewhere.

(b)

The areas must total 1:

\[k\int_0^2x^2dx+k\int_2^6(6-x)dx=k\left(\frac83+8\right)=1.\]

Thus \(k=3/32\).

(c)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(0\le x\lt 2\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{3 u^{2}}{32}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u^{3}}{32}\right]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{3}}{32}\]

Include the accumulated probability \(\frac{1}{4}\) from the earlier interval for \(2\le x\lt 6\):

\[F(x)=\frac{1}{4}+\int_{2}^{x}\frac{3 \left(6 - u\right)}{32}\,du=\frac{1}{4}+\left[\frac{3 u \left(12 - u\right)}{64}\right]_{2}^{x}=1-\frac{3(6-x)^2}{64}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{3}}{32},&0\le x\lt 2\\1-\frac{3(6-x)^2}{64},&2\le x\lt 6\\1,&x\ge 6.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(d)

Since \(F(2)=1/4\), the median lies in the second branch. Its upper tail has probability

\[\mathrm P(X\gt m)=\frac3{64}(6-m)^2.\]

Set this to \(1/2\):

\[(6-m)^2=\frac{32}3,\qquad m=6-\frac{4\sqrt6}3.\]

The plus sign would put the median beyond 6 and is rejected.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Compare the two heights at the joining value.

(b)

Use integration for the curved part and a triangle area or an integral for the linear part.

(c)

The first branch carries probability \(1/4\).

(d)

Use the right-tail triangle once you have located the median.

questions.title: A finite reciprocal moment
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}kx^2,&0\le x\lt1,\\k(2x+1),&1\le x\le2,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find \(k\).

    [2]

  2. Find the cumulative distribution function.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact median.

    [2]

  4. Find \(\mathrm E(1/X)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[k=\frac3{13}.\]

(b)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{3}}{13},&0\le x\lt 1\\\frac{3 x^{2} + 3 x - 5}{13},&1\le x\lt 2\\1,&x\ge 2.\end{cases}\]

(c)

\[\frac{-3 + 7 \sqrt{3}}{6}\]

(d)

\[\frac{3 \left(2 \ln{\left(2 \right)} + 5\right)}{26}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Normalisation gives

\[k\int_0^1x^2dx+k\int_1^2(2x+1)dx=k\left(\frac13+4\right)=1.\]

Hence \(k=3/13\). The density has a jump at 1, which is allowed.

(b)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(0\le x\lt 1\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{3 u^{2}}{13}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u^{3}}{13}\right]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{3}}{13}\]

Include the accumulated probability \(\frac{1}{13}\) from the earlier interval for \(1\le x\lt 2\):

\[F(x)=\frac{1}{13}+\int_{1}^{x}\frac{3 \left(2 u + 1\right)}{13}\,du=\frac{1}{13}+\left[\frac{3 u \left(u + 1\right)}{13}\right]_{1}^{x}=\frac{3 x^{2} + 3 x - 5}{13}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{3}}{13},&0\le x\lt 1\\\frac{3 x^{2} + 3 x - 5}{13},&1\le x\lt 2\\1,&x\ge 2.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(c)

Because \(F(1)=1/13\lt1/2\), set the second branch equal to \(1/2\):

\[\frac{3m^2+3m-5}{13}=\frac12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad6m^2+6m-23=0.\]

The root in \([1,2]\) is

\[m=\frac{-3 + 7 \sqrt{3}}{6}.\]

(d)

Use the expectation integral; the value of \(1/X\) at the single point \(X=0\) has no effect. Near zero, \(f(x)/x=3x/13\), which is integrable. Thus

\[\mathrm E(1/X)=\frac3{13}\int_0^1x\,dx+\frac3{13}\int_1^2\left(2+\frac1x\right)dx =\frac3{13}\left(\frac52+\ln2\right).\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate both non-negative pieces.

(b)

At the join, the accumulated probability is \(1/13\).

(c)

The lower-support branch contains too little probability to contain the median.

(d)

Cancel one factor of x in the first density branch before integrating.

questions.title: A square-root substitution
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac1{34}\left(3\sqrt x-\frac2{\sqrt x}\right),&4\le x\le9,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. The variable \(Y\) is defined by \(Y=\sqrt X\). Find its probability density function.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 4\\\frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}} - 2 \sqrt{x} - 4}{17},&4\le x\lt 9\\1,&x\ge 9.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{3 y^{2} - 2}{17},&2\le y\le 3\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(4\le x\lt 9\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{4}^{x}\frac{3 \sqrt{u} - \frac{2}{\sqrt{u}}}{34}\,du=0+\left[\frac{\sqrt{u} \left(u - 2\right)}{17}\right]_{4}^{x}=\frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}} - 2 \sqrt{x} - 4}{17}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 4\\\frac{x^{\frac{3}{2}} - 2 \sqrt{x} - 4}{17},&4\le x\lt 9\\1,&x\ge 9.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(b)

The transformation \(Y=\sqrt{X}\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(2\le Y\le3\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\ley^{2})=F(y^{2}).\]

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 2\\\frac{y^{3} - 2 y - 4}{17},&2\le y\lt 3\\1,&y\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{3 y^{2} - 2}{17},&2\le y\le 3\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Integrate from 4 and check that the result is 1 at 9.

(b)

Find \(G(y)=F(y^2)\) on \(2\le y\le3\), then differentiate.

questions.title: A decreasing reciprocal transformation
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac1{10}\left(x^2+\frac2{x^2}\right),&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. The variable \(Y\) is defined by \(Y=1/X\). Find the probability density function of \(Y\).

    [4]

  3. Find the 80th percentile of \(Y\), correct to 3 significant figures.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac1{30}\left(x^3-\frac6x+5\right),&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{2 + \frac{1}{y^{4}}}{10},&\frac{1}{3}\le y\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(c)

\[0.601.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(1\le x\lt 3\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{1}^{x}\frac{u^{2} + \frac{2}{u^{2}}}{10}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u^{3} - \frac{6}{u}}{30}\right]_{1}^{x}=\frac1{30}\left(x^3-\frac6x+5\right)\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac1{30}\left(x^3-\frac6x+5\right),&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(b)

The transformation \(Y=\frac{1}{X}\) is decreasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(\frac{1}{3}\le Y\le1\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\ge\frac{1}{y})=1-F(\frac{1}{y}).\]

Because the transformation is decreasing, the inequality reverses. Since \(X\) is continuous, either endpoint convention gives the same tail probability.

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt \frac{1}{3}\\\frac{6 y + 25 - \frac{1}{y^{3}}}{30},&\frac{1}{3}\le y\lt 1\\1,&y\ge 1.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{2 + \frac{1}{y^{4}}}{10},&\frac{1}{3}\le y\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

(c)

Within the support, the CDF of \(Y\) is

\[G(y)=\frac{25+6y-y^{-3}}{30}.\]

For the 80th percentile \(q\), set \(G(q)=4/5\). Multiplying by \(30q^3\) yields

\[6q^4+q^3-1=0.\]

questions.title: A shifted square
questions.prompt_html:
The CDF of \(X\) is

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt0,\\\frac{x^2+2x^4}{36},&0\le x\lt2,\\1,&x\ge2.\end{cases}\]

Let \(Y=X^2+1\).

  1. Find the probability density function of \(Y\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(Y)\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{4 y - 3}{36},&1\le y\le 5\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[\frac{97}{27}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The transformation \(Y=X^{2} + 1\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(1\le Y\le5\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\le\sqrt{y - 1})=F(\sqrt{y - 1}).\]

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\\frac{2 y^{2} - 3 y + 1}{36},&1\le y\lt 5\\1,&y\ge 5.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{4 y - 3}{36},&1\le y\le 5\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

(b)

Use the density from part (a):

\[\mathrm E(Y)=\int_1^5 y\frac{4y-3}{36}dy =\left[\frac{y^3}{27}-\frac{y^2}{24}\right]_1^5=\frac{97}{27}.\]

As a check, the same result follows from \(\mathrm E(Y)=\mathrm E(X^2)+1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Solve \(Y\le y\) for the non-negative variable \(X\).

(b)

The transformed support is \([1,5]\).

questions.title: A shifted cube and its median
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}(x+1)/6,&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. Let \(Y=(X+1)^3\). Find the probability density function of \(Y\).

    [4]

  3. Find the exact median of \(Y\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac{x^{2} + 2 x - 3}{12},&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{18 \sqrt[3]{y}},&8\le y\le 64\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(c)

\[10 \sqrt{10}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(1\le x\lt 3\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{1}^{x}\frac{u + 1}{6}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u \left(u + 2\right)}{12}\right]_{1}^{x}=\frac{x^{2} + 2 x - 3}{12}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac{x^{2} + 2 x - 3}{12},&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(b)

The transformation \(Y=\left(X + 1\right)^{3}\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(8\le Y\le64\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\le\sqrt[3]{y} - 1)=F(\sqrt[3]{y} - 1).\]

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 8\\\frac{y^{\frac{2}{3}} - 4}{12},&8\le y\lt 64\\1,&y\ge 64.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{18 \sqrt[3]{y}},&8\le y\le 64\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

(c)

For \(8\le y\le64\),

\[G(y)=\frac{y^{2/3}-4}{12}.\]

At the median \(m\),

\[\frac{m^{2/3}-4}{12}=\frac12\quad\Longrightarrow\quad m^{2/3}=10.\]

Since \(m\gt0\),

\[m=10^{3/2}=10\sqrt{10}.\]

It lies between 8 and 64, as required.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The antiderivative is most conveniently expressed using \((x+1)^2\).

(b)

First find the range of \((X+1)^3\).

(c)

An increasing transformation maps the median of X to the median of Y.

questions.title: From an exponential density to a bounded variable
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}ae^{-3x\ln2},&x\ge0,\\0,&x\lt0,\end{cases}\]

where \(a\gt0\).

  1. Find \(a\).

    [2]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(X)\), showing an integration argument.

    [2]

  3. Find the exact interquartile range of \(X\).

    [3]

  4. Let \(Y=2^{-X}\). Find the CDF and PDF of \(Y\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=3\ln2.\]

(b)

\[\frac{1}{3 \ln{\left(2 \right)}}\]

(c)

\[\frac{\ln3}{3\ln2}.\]

(d)

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\y^{3},&0\le y\lt 1\\1,&y\ge 1.\end{cases}\]
\[g(y)=\begin{cases}3 y^{2},&0\le y\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Normalisation gives

\[1=\int_0^\infty ae^{-3x\ln2}dx=\frac a{3\ln2}.\]

Hence \(a=3\ln2\). The exponential decay makes the improper integral convergent.

(b)

Let \(\lambda=3\ln2\). Integration by parts gives

\[\mathrm E(X)=\int_0^\infty x\lambda e^{-\lambda x}dx =\left[-xe^{-\lambda x}\right]_0^\infty+\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda x}dx =\frac1\lambda=\frac1{3\ln2}.\]

The boundary term vanishes because \(xe^{-\lambda x}\to0\).

(c)

The CDF is \(F(x)=1-e^{-3x\ln2}\) for \(x\ge0\). Therefore

\[Q_1=\frac{\ln(4/3)}{3\ln2},\qquad Q_3=\frac{\ln4}{3\ln2}.\]

Subtract using the logarithm law:

\[Q_3-Q_1=\frac{\ln4-\ln(4/3)}{3\ln2}=\frac{\ln3}{3\ln2}.\]

(d)

The transformation \(Y=2^{- X}\) is decreasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(0\lt Y\le1\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\ge- \frac{\ln{\left(y \right)}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}})=1-F(- \frac{\ln{\left(y \right)}}{\ln{\left(2 \right)}}).\]

Because the transformation is decreasing, the inequality reverses. Since \(X\) is continuous, either endpoint convention gives the same tail probability.

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\y^{3},&0\le y\lt 1\\1,&y\ge 1.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}3 y^{2},&0\le y\le 1\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

In particular, for \(0\lt y\lt1\),

\[G(y)=e^{-3\ln2\,(-\ln y/\ln2)}=y^3.\]

There is no point mass at either endpoint: the CDF is continuous at 0 and 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the total integral of the density.

(b)

Integrate by parts; do not assume a memorised mean.

(c)

Solve the two CDF equations before subtracting.

(d)

The transformation is decreasing, so use a survival probability after taking logarithms.

questions.title: Moments after taking a square root
questions.prompt_html:
A random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac1{10}\left(4-\frac1{\sqrt x}\right),&1\le x\le4,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The variable \(Y\) is defined by \(Y=\sqrt X\).

  1. Find the probability density function of \(Y\), using a CDF argument.

    [4]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(Y)\).

    [3]

  3. Find \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{4 y - 1}{5},&1\le y\le 2\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[\frac{47}{30}\]

(c)

\[\frac{71}{900}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(1\le x\lt 4\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{1}^{x}\frac{4 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}}{10}\,du=0+\left[\frac{- \sqrt{u} + 2 u}{5}\right]_{1}^{x}=\frac{- \sqrt{x} + 2 x - 1}{5}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 1\\\frac{- \sqrt{x} + 2 x - 1}{5},&1\le x\lt 4\\1,&x\ge 4.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

The transformation \(Y=\sqrt{X}\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(1\le Y\le2\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\ley^{2})=F(y^{2}).\]

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\\frac{2 y^{2} - y - 1}{5},&1\le y\lt 2\\1,&y\ge 2.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{4 y - 1}{5},&1\le y\le 2\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

(b)

Integrating over the transformed support gives

\[\mathrm E(Y)=\frac15\int_1^2 y(4y-1)dy =\frac15\left[\frac{4y^3}3-\frac{y^2}2\right]_1^2=\frac{47}{30}.\]

Equivalently this is \(\mathrm E(\sqrt X)\), computed directly from the original density.

(c)

The second moment is

\[\mathrm E(Y^2)=\frac15\int_1^2 y^2(4y-1)dy=\frac{38}{15}.\]

Hence

\[\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\frac{38}{15}-\left(\frac{47}{30}\right)^2=\frac{71}{900}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

First integrate f to get F, then substitute \(x=y^2\).

(b)

Use the density of Y and limits 1 and 2.

(c)

Calculate \(\mathrm E(Y^2)\); it also equals \(\mathrm E(X)\).

questions.title: A square root across a density break
questions.prompt_html:
The density of \(X\) is

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac{\sqrt x}{54},&0\le x\lt9,\\\frac1{k\sqrt x},&9\le x\le16,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\]

where \(k\gt0\).

  1. Find \(k\).

    [2]

  2. Find the exact median of \(X\).

    [3]

  3. Let \(Y=\sqrt X-1\). Find the CDF and PDF of \(Y\).

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[k=3.\]

(b)

\[\frac{169}{16}.\]

(c)

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt -1\\\frac{(y+1)^3}{81},&-1\le y\lt 2\\\frac{2 y}{3} - 1,&2\le y\lt 3\\1,&y\ge 3.\end{cases}\]
\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\left(y + 1\right)^{2}}{27},&-1\le y\lt 2\\\frac{2}{3},&2\le y\le 3\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The first branch has probability

\[\int_0^9\frac{\sqrt x}{54}dx=\frac1{54}\left[\frac23x^{3/2}\right]_0^9=\frac13.\]

The second branch has probability \((2/k)(4-3)=2/k\). Thus \(1/3+2/k=1\), giving \(k=3\).

(b)

Since the first branch has mass \(1/3\lt1/2\), the median is in \([9,16]\):

\[\frac13+\int_9^m\frac1{3\sqrt x}dx=\frac12.\]

Hence

\[\frac13+\frac23(\sqrt m-3)=\frac12,\qquad \sqrt m=\frac{13}{4},\qquad m=\frac{169}{16}.\]

This is indeed between 9 and 16.

(c)

The transformation \(Y=\sqrt{X} - 1\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(-1\le Y\le3\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\le\left(y + 1\right)^{2})=F(\left(y + 1\right)^{2}).\]

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt -1\\\frac{(y+1)^3}{81},&-1\le y\lt 2\\\frac{2 y}{3} - 1,&2\le y\lt 3\\1,&y\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{\left(y + 1\right)^{2}}{27},&-1\le y\lt 2\\\frac{2}{3},&2\le y\le 3\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

The support of \(Y\) starts at \(-1\), not at 0. The original break \(X=9\) becomes \(Y=2\). For the first piece, \(G(y)=(y+1)^3/81\); for the second, \(G(y)=(2y-3)/3\).

(a)

Use the total probability, not continuity of the density.

(b)

Add the first-branch mass before solving the median equation.

(c)

questions.title: Does a square root increase the median?
questions.prompt_html:
A continuous random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac23x,&0\le x\lt1,\\\frac14(3-x)^2,&1\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find the cumulative distribution function of \(X\).

    [3]

  2. Find the exact median \(m_X\).

    [2]

  3. Let \(Y=\sqrt X\). Find the cumulative distribution function of \(Y\).

    [3]

  4. Determine, with justification, whether the median of \(Y\) is greater than or less than \(m_X\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{2}}{3},&0\le x\lt 1\\1-\frac{(3-x)^3}{12},&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

(b)

\[3 - \sqrt[3]{6}\]

(c)

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\\frac{y^{4}}{3},&0\le y\lt 1\\1-\frac{(3-y^2)^3}{12},&1\le y\lt \sqrt{3}\\1,&y\ge \sqrt{3}.\end{cases}\]

(d)

The median of \(Y\) is smaller: \(m_Y=\sqrt{3-\sqrt[3]6}\lt m_X\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Integrate from the lower support endpoint for \(0\le x\lt 1\):

\[F(x)=0+\int_{0}^{x}\frac{2 u}{3}\,du=0+\left[\frac{u^{2}}{3}\right]_{0}^{x}=\frac{x^{2}}{3}\]

Include the accumulated probability \(\frac{1}{3}\) from the earlier interval for \(1\le x\lt 3\):

\[F(x)=\frac{1}{3}+\int_{1}^{x}\frac{\left(3 - u\right)^{2}}{4}\,du=\frac{1}{3}+\left[\frac{u \left(u^{2} - 9 u + 27\right)}{12}\right]_{1}^{x}=1-\frac{(3-x)^3}{12}\]

Outside the support the CDF is 0 below the lower endpoint and 1 above the upper endpoint. Hence

\[F(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\lt 0\\\frac{x^{2}}{3},&0\le x\lt 1\\1-\frac{(3-x)^3}{12},&1\le x\lt 3\\1,&x\ge 3.\end{cases}\]

The pieces meet continuously, and the CDF is non-decreasing from 0 to 1.

(b)

Since \(F(1)=1/3\), use the second branch:

\[1-\frac{(3-m_X)^3}{12}=\frac12.\]

Thus \((3-m_X)^3=6\) and

\[m_X=3-\sqrt[3]6.\]

(c)

Because the square root is increasing on \(X\ge0\),

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(X\le y^2)=F(y^2).\]

The endpoints 0 and 3 become 0 and \(\sqrt3\), while the breakpoint remains 1. Therefore

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\\frac{y^{4}}{3},&0\le y\lt 1\\1-\frac{(3-y^2)^3}{12},&1\le y\lt \sqrt{3}\\1,&y\ge \sqrt{3}.\end{cases}.\]

(d)

An increasing transformation maps the unique median to the transformed median:

\[m_Y=\sqrt{m_X}.\]

Since \(6\lt8\), we have \(\sqrt[3]6\lt2\), so \(m_X=3-\sqrt[3]6\gt1\). For a number greater than 1, its square root is smaller. Hence

\[m_Y=\sqrt{3-\sqrt[3]6}\lt3-\sqrt[3]6=m_X.\]

questions.prompt_html:
A continuous random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}a,&0\le x\lt3,\\b-cx,&3\le x\le7,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is continuous at \(x=3\), and the linear section reaches height zero at \(x=7\).

  1. Find \(a,b,c\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(\mathrm E(X)\).

    [3]

  3. Find the median of \(X\).

    [1]

  4. Let \(Y=(X+1)^2\). Find the cumulative distribution function of \(Y\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=\frac15,\qquad b=\frac7{20},\qquad c=\frac1{20}.\]

(b)

\[\frac{79}{30}.\]

(c)

\[\frac52.\]

(d)

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\\frac{\sqrt{y} - 1}{5},&1\le y\lt 16\\1-\frac{(8-\sqrt y)^2}{40},&16\le y\lt 64\\1,&y\ge 64.\end{cases}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The endpoint condition gives \(b-7c=0\). Continuity gives \(a=b-3c=4c\). The total area consists of a rectangle and a triangle:

\[3a+\frac12(7-3)a=5a=1.\]

Hence \(a=1/5\), \(c=a/4=1/20\), and \(b=7c=7/20\). These conditions determine the model without relying on an omitted diagram.

(b)

Use the two density pieces:

\[\mathrm E(X)=\frac15\int_0^3x\,dx+\frac1{20}\int_3^7x(7-x)dx.\]
\[=\frac9{10}+\frac1{20}\left[\frac{7x^2}{2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_3^7 =\frac9{10}+\frac{26}{15}=\frac{79}{30}.\]

(c)

The plateau contains mass \(3/5\gt1/2\), so the median is on that interval. Since \(F(m)=m/5\), the equation \(m/5=1/2\) gives \(m=5/2\).

(d)

The CDF of \(X\) on its support is \(x/5\) up to 3, then \(1-(7-x)^2/40\). Since \(X+1\gt0\),

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(X\le\sqrt y-1)=F(\sqrt y-1).\]

The values \(X=0,3,7\) correspond to \(Y=1,16,64\). Substitution gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 1\\\frac{\sqrt{y} - 1}{5},&1\le y\lt 16\\1-\frac{(8-\sqrt y)^2}{40},&16\le y\lt 64\\1,&y\ge 64.\end{cases}.\]

At \(y=16\), both interior branches equal \(3/5\), providing a continuity check.

\[10-\sqrt{34}.\]

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{3 y^{2} \left(y^{3} - 1\right)}{34},&1\le y\lt \sqrt[3]{3}\\\frac{3 y^{2} \left(11 - y^{3}\right)}{34},&\sqrt[3]{3}\le y\le \sqrt[3]{11}\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

\[\frac1{34}\int_m^{10}(10-x)dx=\frac{(10-m)^2}{68}=\frac12.\]

\[m=10-\sqrt{34}.\]

The transformation \(Y=\sqrt[3]{X + 1}\) is increasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(1\le Y\le\sqrt[3]{11}\).

questions.title: A reflected square
questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has density

\[f(x)=\begin{cases}\frac4{81}x(9-x^2),&0\le x\le3,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

  1. Find \(\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)\).

    [4]

  2. Let \(Y=9-X^2\). Find the probability density function of \(Y\), using a CDF argument.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact median of \(Y\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{56}{675}.\]

(b)

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{2 y}{81},&0\le y\le 9\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

(c)

\[\frac{9 \sqrt{2}}{2}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

First calculate the mean of \(\sqrt X\):

\[\mathrm E(\sqrt X)=\frac4{81}\int_0^3(9x^{3/2}-x^{7/2})dx =\frac4{81}\left[\frac{18}{5}x^{5/2}-\frac29x^{9/2}\right]_0^3 =\frac{32\sqrt3}{45}.\]

The second moment of \(\sqrt X\) is

\[\mathrm E(X)=\frac4{81}\int_0^3(9x^2-x^4)dx=\frac85.\]

Consequently

\[\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)=\frac85-\left(\frac{32\sqrt3}{45}\right)^2=\frac{56}{675}.\]

(b)

The transformation \(Y=9 - X^{2}\) is decreasing on the support of \(X\). Mapping the endpoints gives \(0\le Y\le9\).

For \(y\) within this range,

\[G(y)=\mathrm P(Y\le y)=\mathrm P(X\ge\sqrt{9 - y})=1-F(\sqrt{9 - y}).\]

Because the transformation is decreasing, the inequality reverses. Since \(X\) is continuous, either endpoint convention gives the same tail probability.

Substituting separately into the appropriate branches of the original CDF gives

\[G(y)=\begin{cases}0,&y\lt 0\\\frac{y^{2}}{81},&0\le y\lt 9\\1,&y\ge 9.\end{cases}\]

Differentiate each non-constant branch with respect to \(y\):

\[g(y)=\begin{cases}\frac{2 y}{81},&0\le y\le 9\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\]

The density is zero elsewhere. Values assigned to a density at isolated endpoints do not affect probabilities.

(c)

From part (b), \(G(y)=y^2/81\) for \(0\le y\le9\). At the median,

\[\frac{m^2}{81}=\frac12.\]

The support is non-negative, so

\[m=\frac9{\sqrt2}=\frac{9\sqrt2}{2}.\]

The negative root is excluded.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Calculate \(\mathrm E(\sqrt X)\) and \(\mathrm E(X)\), not \(\mathrm E(X^2)\).

(b)

The map decreases from 9 to 0 as X increases from 0 to 3.

(c)

Use the CDF of Y, not that of X.
